$$

after.worked_solution:
If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y)=(0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & ={e}^{x-2y}, & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =-2{e}^{x-2y} \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =1, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & ={e}^{x-2y}, & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =1 \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =-2{e}^{x-2y}, & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =-2 \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =4{e}^{x-2y}, & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈1+1\cdot x+(-2)\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}(1\cdot {x}^{2}+2(-2)\cdot xy+4\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =1+x+(-2)y+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+(-2)xy+2{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=(-2)+(-2)+2=-2.
$$

after.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the first derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y & \frac{x}{y}+x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{1}{y}+1 \\ \frac{1}{y}+1 & -\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$

$$

Suppose that the function f:Rn→R is defined by

f:[x1x2⋮xn]⟶z

and is twice differentiable at x=a. Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of f about a is given by

f(x)≈f(a)+f′(a)(x−a)+12(x−a)Tf″(a)(x−a),

where

f′(a)=[∂f∂x1∂f∂x2⋯∂f∂xn]|x=a

and

f″(a)=[∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x1∂xn∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯∂2f∂x2∂xn⋮⋮⋮⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1∂2f∂xn∂x2⋯∂2f∂xn2]x=a

In this case, we have the following:

f′(x)=[∂f∂x∂f∂y],f″(x)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2]

Calculating the first derivative, we have

f′(x)=[3(x−y)2−3(x−y)2].

Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

f″(x)=[6(x−y)−6(x−y)−6(x−y)6(x−y)]f″(0,1)=[−666−6]

f(x)≈f(a)+f′(a)(x−a)+12[xy−1]T[−666−6][xy−1].

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

x+6+(y−1)=x+y+5.

content.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the first derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}3(x-y)^{2} & -3(x-y)^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}6(x-y) & -6(x-y) \\ -6(x-y) & 6(x-y)\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(0,1) & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 6 \\ 6 & -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-6 & 6 \\ 6 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y-1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
x+6+(y-1)=x+y+5.
$$

the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$
after.worked_solution:
If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y)=(0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{x-y+1}, & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{x-y+1} \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =1, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{(x-y+1)^{2}}, & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =-1 \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{(x-y+1)^{2}}, & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =1 \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{(x-y+1)^{2}}, & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈0+1\cdot x+(-1)\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}(-1\cdot {x}^{2}+2(1)\cdot xy+(-1)\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =1x-y-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+1xy+(-\frac{1}{2}){y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=1+1+(-\frac{1}{2})=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

For the function of two variables 
$f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-y+1),$
the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=ax-y-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+bxy+c{y}^{2}.
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$
content.worked_solution:
If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y)=(0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{x-y+1}, & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{x-y+1} \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =1, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{(x-y+1)^{2}}, & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =-1 \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{(x-y+1)^{2}}, & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =1 \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{(x-y+1)^{2}}, & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈0+1\cdot x+(-1)\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}(-1\cdot {x}^{2}+2(1)\cdot xy+(-1)\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =1x-y-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+1xy+(-\frac{1}{2}){y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=1+1+(-\frac{1}{2})=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

after.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =3, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈3+[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,2) & ≈3+[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}1-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =3+[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =3+(-2)+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =1+\frac{1}{2}(4) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$
